The *Lengyan Shuzhi* (An Exposition of the Essential Meaning of the Śūraṅgama): This work expounds the essential meaning of the Buddha, the King of Awakening; it reiterates and explains its significance. One might ask:

"Since the meaning has already been explained, is it not redundant to reiterate and explain it again? I reply: "The Buddha, the King of Awakening, is far removed in time; we are unable to hear his teachings directly.
When the First Council was held at the Jeta Grove, Ānanda recorded them; thus, this is Ānanda’s *Śūraṅgama*."
Translated in India, it was the *Śūraṅgama* of Prajñāmitra; translated again in Oḍḍiyāna, it was the *Śūraṅgama* of Meghaśikṣa.
Transmitted to China, with Fang Gong, the Chancellor, acting as the scribe, it became the *Śūraṅgama* of Fang Gong the Chancellor—all of these are expositions.
The languages of the barbarians and India are expressed through indirectness, whereas those of China—

Now, when a guest floats above the host, even a tutor cannot overcome the influence of those who distract him; how much more so when one attempts to explain the "Scripture of Ying" with the theories of "Yan"?
The term *jīng* (sūtra) means "direct path. By following its text, one takes the direct route to grasp its essential meaning; that is sufficient. I, being lacking in talent, have once said:

The distance is already great. Furthermore, excessive words obscure the Way, and excessive learning drowns the mind. To provide ten proofs for a single point is not as effective as a rare analogy.
The Master said: "I wish to remain without words; let the expression suffice. What is easy is easily known; what is concise is easily understood.
When ease and simplicity are attained, the principles of the world are grasped. How could the intention of the Awakened King (the Buddha) be otherwise?

by pruning away the superfluous, the branches and trunk reach full development; by clearing away obstructions, the veins and channels flow like rivers.
Have you not observed the butcher Ding as he dissects oxen? By following the natural tendons and sinews, his blade moves with effortless ease. Thus I proclaim the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Volume One: Collection of Characters Beginning with "Jing" (淨).
Chapter One: Examining the Mind.
At the outset, Ānanda took the mind that delights in the conditions of seeing and form as the fundamental thought for renouncing his body to study the Way.
Since the ground was already not true, it was only natural that demonic realms would appear before him and he could not liberate himself; all of this was due to conditions.
The delusion of thought secretly nourishes and grows within the hidden and subtle, causing you confusion; the eyes and mind are at fault.
The Buddha, wishing to uplift Ānanda, caused him to directly investigate the source of the eyes and mind. Ānanda reflected upon this repeatedly.

Ultimately, one realizes the Buddha-nature for oneself. Through successive and profound analysis, the Buddha demonstrates that this mind of conscious cognition is entirely illusory and is not the true mind.
This constitutes the beginning of the teaching of this sutra; it is the first chapter, "Inquiry into the Mind."
Chapter Two: Distinguishing Views.
Because Ānanda had failed to attain realization through each of the seven preceding inquiries, he earnestly entreated [the Buddha], seeking to reach the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The Buddha, for the sake of discerning the real from the false, said: "You now grasp at this mind that clings to objects as being your own self-nature, just as you previously saw me."
Seeing these excellent marks, he immediately gave rise to attachment and delight, not realizing that this was the fundamental luminosity of the essence of consciousness.

It seizes upon the eyes and manifests through the mind; it is capable of perceiving all objects. Because it perceives objects, it becomes deluded and, conversely, abandons its true nature. Consequently, [the Buddha] raised his palm and projected a light, asking, "What do you see?
Ānanda replied, "I see with my eyes. Thus, he believed that the capacity to see resides in the eyes and that the power of discernment [resides there].

You take this to be the mind, yet you do not know that it is entirely a shadow of external objects and conditions—a false conceptualization that deludes your true mind, arising and ceasing like a phantom.
Therefore, the Buddha rebuked it as not being real and used the "eight returns" to dismantle it, saying: "This essence of seeing depends upon objects;
when the object passes, the seeing returns. It is like a traveler lodging in an inn; it is certainly not a permanent residence. You must...

To know and see that the nature of seeing exists, yet it is not the eye that sees: when the external objects before one are seen, they perish along with their cessation; both belong to illusory delusion.
To understand these conditions of objects and no longer undergo agitation or confusion, one will naturally be free from the cycle of rebirth. However, this has not yet pointed to the True Mind;
it is merely a provisional means to distinguish the nature of seeing.
Volume Two: The Collection of the Character "Ji" (極).
Section Three: The True Nature is Permanently Abiding.
Ānanda realized for himself that since time immemorial, he had lost his original mind and mistakenly identified with the shadows of external conditions; he relied only upon the present...
The former perishes and ceases; it is renewed moment by moment and does not abide. How, then, can one attain the eternally abiding true mind that is not subject to transformation or extinction?
In response to King Prasenajit’s question, the Buddha provisionally used the perception of the river as a window to illuminate his understanding.

If one says that although the child and the old man differ in age, the perception of the river remains as it was yesterday, then since this perception does not change, it can be known that it does not perish. A...
[The interlocutor] spoke with difficulty: "This essence of vision must be my true nature; it is eternally abiding. Why then do you say that I have lost it?
The Buddha said: "Your perception is inverted; therefore, you have lost it. He then used the metaphor of his outstretched arm, saying:

"The substance of the arm is originally one, yet because of its upward or downward orientation, one's view of it changes. Thus, within your state of neither sameness nor difference, [the essence] blazes forth into existence."
As for this difference, is it not caused by your own inverted views? You do not realize that the source of the Buddha’s Dharma-body is fundamentally non-dual.

Due to delusion based on false conditions, you lose track of the Truth and call this state "inversion. You take the obscured and dark as emptiness, and the congealed darkness as form. By binding thoughts, you create a body;
internally agitated and externally distracted, you remain mired in a state of confused turmoil, confined within the limits of the physical body. Now...
You take this to be your own mind; how could you know that the wondrously luminous true mind completely envelops the ten voids?
It is like taking a single bubble from a clear, vast ocean of hundreds of thousands of leagues to be the entire ocean—is this not delusion?

Once you understand this, the distinction between the true mind and the conditioned mind will naturally be discerned as real and false. This is just like Ānanda, who used his conditioned mind to listen to the Dharma. Furthermore—
"Please resolve my doubts. The Buddha said: "You listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind and take that to be the true mind.

You must depart from the sensory object of sound; there must be a faculty of hearing that exists apart from it, which alone constitutes the true mind. Now, because you exist due to sound, you cease to exist when separated from sound."
It is ultimately not the permanent resident who never returns, like the master of a guest inn. It is just as there can be no second sun in the sky:

that which is created by squeezing the sun away ceases to exist when the squeezing stops; it is certainly not the true sun. Know, therefore, that all things which can be returned are naturally not you.
That which cannot be returned to you is not you, yet it deceives you. If you do not return [to it], it is naturally and eternally abiding.
Chapter Four: Distinguishing the Non-Buddhist Paths.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s words above, [noted that] awakening pervades the ten directions and the true nature is eternally abiding. He asked:
"How does this differ from the 'True Self' (ātman) taught by the non-Buddhists? The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Those non-Buddhists constantly speak of spontaneity (svabhāva)."
"What I speak of as causes and conditions is not their realm. Now, observe that the nature of awareness is spontaneous; it is neither born nor extinguished.

It seems that what is 'not caused by conditions' and that which is 'spontaneous' are one and the same. How should this be explained? The Buddha said: "That which is called 'spontaneous' means that there is a self-originated spontaneity.
If there is a self-originated spontaneity, then that which is 'self' must necessarily possess an essential nature (*svabhāva*). Only..."
This wondrous, luminous true mind permeates heaven and becomes heaven; it permeates earth and becomes earth.
Fundamentally, it has no fixed location, nor does it depend upon or cling to material objects. Since it possesses no fixed location, can one take this luminosity as one's own self?
Does it take emptiness as its own nature? Since it is free from all dependence and attachment, does it exist because of things, or does it abide by means of things?
Therefore, it is neither caused nor conditioned, yet it is not uncaused or unconditioned; there is nothing that is not so, and thus it is not "not-so.
There is nothing that is so, and thus it is not "so. It is detached from all marks and cannot be contained within them.
It is cessation; that is, all dharmas do not admit of attachment. Such is the nature of its essence.

Originally, it is not something that can be conjectured through the verbal explanations of non-Buddhists. Yet worldly people say, "My capacity for vision exists within brightness, darkness, emptiness, and obstruction.
They do not realize that these all belong to the conditioned objects (*ālambana*) and are ultimately not the substance of seeing itself. One must necessarily...
When one sees the seeing by being free from dust, one should further know that at the moment of seeing the seeing, this seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.
This seeing of the seeing is precisely the seeing that is detached from objects, rather than the seeing that clings to objects. Such is the essence of true seeing.
It is already beyond the reach of views; how much more so could it be reached by any verbal expression, such as "caused by conditions," "arising spontaneously," or "harmonious conjunction"?
Therefore, the subsequent section concludes by stating that [such] views are delusive.
Chapter Five: On the Delusion of Views.
When the awakening consciousness perceives various objects and gives rise to discrimination, this is called the delusion of views.

It is like a person whose eyes suffer from the disease of cataracts and sees circular halos around lamp lights with five overlapping colors; yet although the eyes have the disease, they are still able to see that these [halos] exist.
As for those with the disease of optical aberration, my fundamentally awakened, luminous mind is inherently free from disease;
it does not undergo the disease of aberration. If the disease of aberration is removed, true awakening naturally returns.

Thus, your perception of the various false phenomena of the world—the mountains, rivers, great earth, lands, and sentient beings—may also be said to be produced by the beginningless disease of seeing. Why is this so?

Therefore, because they are equally devoid of substantial reality, and furthermore, because the deluded perceptions of the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) resulting from three kinds of distinct karmas are clarified through both progressive and regressive analysis:
when one person suffers from an eye ailment, a circular halo appears around a lamp; when an entire country is afflicted by pestilence, calamities arise simultaneously.

Seeing the halo and seeing the calamity, both ultimately revert to unreality. By this analogy, the lands and sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm are likewise [manifestations of] the self-awakened clarity.
The untainted, wondrous mind gives rise to delusion based upon the Truth; both alike fall into the sickness of views, and none are able to remove it.

If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction as well as all non-conjoined phenomena, then one can extinguish the causes of birth and death, perfect the nature of bodhi which is neither born nor extinguished, and the fundamental enlightenment will abide eternally therein.
Chapter Six: Awakening to the Non-Composite Nature.
Ānanda had previously realized that the wondrous clarity of fundamental awakening is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it spontaneous;

yet he still did not understand that this source of awakening is neither produced through combination nor through non-combination, for it is the essence of the awakened mind, while all else is but adventitious dust.
Furthermore, that which is called "discerning awakening" (*vibodha*) emerges from fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*); it is the "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*) that realizes the Way.
Because it is detached from the sense organs and their objects, it is called the "wondrously pure essence of vision. To call this "harmony" (*he*) is like water mixing with soil;
there is no discrimination. To call this "union" (*he*) is like a lid fitting a box; there is no separation. Once there is harmony and union, all [is one].
They belong to the realm of delusory objects and are therefore not wondrously pure. Nevertheless, when the faculties and their objects confront one another, they must either harmonize or conflict;
they must either unite or diverge. If there is even a single instance of non-harmony, then although the essence of vision may be pure, it cannot be called "wondrous.
Only when neither identical nor separate is it truly wondrously pure. Therefore, the following passage reveals the nature of the treasury.
Volume Three: The Collection of the Character "Guang" (光), Chapter Seven:
Manifesting the Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
The Five Aggregates, the Six Bases, the Twelve Entrances, the Eighteen Elements, and the Seven Greats.
Now, within the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is eternally abiding and non-retrogressive; it is neither produced by causes and conditions, nor is it spontaneous;
it is neither a composite nor a conjunction. It stands far beyond the reach of the conceptual deliberations of external paths.

Having thus scrutinized the true and the false and distinguished the heterodox and the orthodox, its meaning is clear and exhaustive. Herein, it is further revealed and demonstrated so that one may know True Suchness.
The wondrous substance pervades the entire Dharma-realm; within the aggregates, bases, and elements, it is manifest in every instance, and every phenomenon is perfectly luminous.
Later, when the seven great elements are extensively cited, they arise in accordance with their respective conditions; there is nothing that is not the wondrous nature of True Suchness.
Nothing whatsoever is excluded. As Mencius said, "All things are fully contained within me. Only after attaining awakening to this can one truly know.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s awakening is vast and boundless; yet one dares not attempt to exhaust the deep seas with a single bubble.

In the eighth chapter, "Verses of Gratitude for Realization," verses are spoken in praise and gratitude, summarizing the preceding meanings: it is said that from time immemorial, we have been deluded regarding the truth and have mistaken conditioned reflections for reality.
The perversion of thought has persisted for more than billions of kalpas. Having once received the Tathāgata’s instruction, I have come to know that wondrous enlightenment is profound and still;
the hidden mind is all-pervasive, eternally abiding and indestructible. The essence and magnitude of this wondrously luminous original mind are such as this.
From this point, I have attained awakening. How does my present body, born of my parents, differ from a mote of dust in the air—existing yet vanishing?

"A great ocean and a floating bubble—do they not arise and perish like illusions? When one’s realization reaches this point, it may be said that they delight in mutual understanding, becoming silent and losing the sense of self.
Having offered these words of praise and gratitude, he further requested that his subtle and minute delusions and hindrances be cleared away;
this serves as the foundation for the subsequent scripture. Indeed, to achieve vastness and exhaust the most refined subtleties is the essential task of the path of cultivation. Previously...
This clarifies the mind that perceives and reveals the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Only then can one shatter the coarse delusions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Next, one must resolve lingering doubts and obstructions to open the gates of cultivation and realization, thereby severing the subtle delusions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Through thorough examination and complete elimination [of these], one ascends to supreme awakening.
Volume Four: Chapter Nine, "Comprehensively Investigating the Profundity of the Myriad Dharmas.
This volume uses Pūrṇa as the occasion for the teaching. Since Pūrṇa was foremost in expounding the Dharma, he is relied upon here to clarify and penetrate [the meaning].
Regarding "doubtful obstructions": The Way of humanity takes the realization of one's nature as its foundation, with the thorough understanding of all phenomena following next.
However, even if one has realized one's nature, if one does not thoroughly understand the myriad phenomena, then one will encounter obstructions at every turn.

Therefore, after the preceding section elucidated the mind and vision to reveal the Tathāgatagarbha, [the Buddha] again employed Pūrṇa to present doubts and exhaustively debate the various conditioned characteristics of the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
One must bring each phenomenon to definitive resolution so that there is no longer any doubt or obstruction; only then can one advance in cultivation and proceed accordingly.

Chapter Ten, "The Threefold Continuity," concerns Pūrṇa’s inquiry following the passage on the seven great elements. Because he had not yet attained understanding of the principle of the sequential arising [of phenomena], he posed two questions. First:

First, one doubts that if the nature of the storehouse (ālayavijñāna) is pure, how can various phenomena arise? Second, one doubts that if the four great elements each pervade all space, how can they coexist within one another?

The Buddha answers: Mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise from deluded awakening; therefore, worlds, empty space, sentient beings, and the fruits of their karma flow on in succession, ending and beginning again in an endless cycle.
He further answers: Form-phenomena are empty of intrinsic reality; their essence is not the same as the manifold phenomena.
Therefore, it is able to refuse nothing as all phenomena unfold. For when one contemplates the nature of these phenomena, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out or described.

Sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses; thus, through form and emptiness, they oppose and usurp one another. Within the Tathāgata-garbha, however, one contemplates that the nature is originally true—merely wondrously luminous awakening.
This wondrously luminous mind of sublime awakening was from the beginning neither water nor fire; how can you demand that it not be so?
Chapter Eleven: On the Exhaustion of the Causes of Delusion.
The continuity of karmic results among the sentient beings of the world all arises from deluded cognition. Purna then asked: "This..."

"From what cause does delusion arise? It obscures one's own wondrous brilliance, leading to this drowning in suffering. The Buddha said, "Wondrous enlightenment is perfectly complete; its nature is fundamentally perfect, bright, and wondrous.
Since it is called 'delusion,' how can there be a cause for it? It is like the case of Pūrṇa, who, terrified of his own head, ran about in a frenzy;
once he realized that his madness had no cause, there was nothing left to extinguish. You need only not follow the karmic fruits of the worldly beings."
When the continuity [of delusion] ceases because the three conditions are severed and the three causes do not arise, then that Pūrṇa’s state of madness will naturally subside.
This subsiding is itself Bodhi; what need is there for arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?
Chapter Twelve: The Externalists’ Doubts Regarding Conditions and Spontaneity.
Ānanda followed the words spoken before him by the Buddha; ultimately, through his great learning, he gave rise to this view:

"If one says that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise—clearly there is a principle of cause and condition—and thus the nature of madness naturally subsides; when it subsides, that is *bodhi*."

If one relies on arduous toil and the cultivation and realization of the "tendons and sinews" (the subtlest parts of the flesh), then this becomes the doctrine of the naturalism of external paths, which constitutes the primary meaning [of the ultimate truth].

Having harbored such doubts and arguments, you requested the Buddha for clarification; yet you did not realize that a great practitioner of the Way understands directly and immediately, such that these [doubts] naturally cease to exist.
One should not add further deliberation, for all verbal expressions are merely frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Therefore, the Buddha...
Furthermore, regarding the matter of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa’s frantic flight, let us exhaustively examine his arguments from two perspectives.

Human beings change and transform in an instant; in the blink of an eye, they travel ten thousand li. When demonic hordes possess the body, they consume and suck away the vital essence.

You must attain foreknowledge to avoid entering the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Fourth, the delusory understandings resulting from the violation of the *dhyāna* of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) (its categories number ten;

As for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): it consists of subtle thoughts and deliberations that continue in an unbroken succession, never remaining still from moment to moment, like a cascading waterfall or a flowing spring.
This is called "hidden delusive conceptualization. When that son of good family has exhausted the aggregate of perceptions (*saṃjñā-skandha*), dreams and waking thoughts are both absent;
he remains constant whether awake or asleep. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky, free once more from the coarse and heavy sensory objects of the external world.

Regarding the phenomenon of shadows: one merely perceives within the profound stillness a flickering, clear agitation. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
When the habit-energy of agitation is extinguished, one returns to the primordial clarity, like waves settling into water, no longer subject to shifting flows.

This transcends the turbidity of sentient beings (where "sentient-being turbidity" refers to the incessant arising and ceasing and the constant transition of karmic movements). From this, the mind becomes concentrated and luminous; thus, Māras find no opportunity to interfere. Therefore, it is said: [the text concludes].

Thereafter, no further demonic activities will arise; however, there is only the danger of losing the proper course while practicing dhyāna, wherein deluded understanding and false conceptualization can cause one to lose right awareness and fall into the ways of external paths. These are ten in number.
1. Within the Perfect Origin, they calculate that there is no cause for the fundamental and the derivative;
2. Within the Perfect Permanence, they calculate four types of partial permanence;
3. Within the Perfect Self and Other, they calculate four types of inversion.
4) Calculating four limits within the various states;
5) Producing evasive and empty discourse regarding knowledge and views;

Tenth, regarding those who calculate five types of nirvana within the subsequent existence (*punarbhava*):

Thus, because the birth and death of all sentient beings were seen to be entirely complete within this [consciousness], he no longer pursued the investigation of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) further.

Thus, humans give birth to humans, and birds give birth to crows. A crow is originally black, and a crane is originally white; they never undergo change.

To speculate in such a manner constitutes the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Because one cultivates the two dharmas of mind and environment, one knows that within twenty thousand kalpas, sentient beings are born and die, and die and are born.
It is like a continuous chain; fundamentally, there is no dispersion or loss. This is to negate arising and ceasing while reckoning [existence] as permanent.

Furthermore, they reckon that the four natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are eternally abiding, and through cultivation, they claim to know that within forty thousand kalpas, the arising and ceasing of sentient beings all possess a constant essence.
This is to maintain arising and ceasing while reckoning [existence] as permanent. Furthermore, they reckon that within the mind, intellect, and consciousness, there is fundamentally...
The nature is eternal; sentient beings rely upon it to cycle through existence without loss. This is to perceive the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) as permanent.

Furthermore, one may reckon that once the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception-aggregate) has been exhausted, there is no further mind of arising and ceasing, and that within the principle of its flowing, halting, and revolving, non-arising and non-ceasing are spontaneously established.
Not knowing that the *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations-aggregate) is the very source of arising and ceasing, one relies on the cessation of perception to make this calculation.
This is permanence. To calculate and deliberate in such a manner is to fall into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, regarding oneself and others, one calculates four inversions (*viparyāsa*): first, falsely establishing a self-soul (*ātman*) that is luminous, immovable, and possesses a permanent nature;

These are those who make distinctions based on their calculations. Second, there are those who depart from their own fundamental mind and universally observe the lands.

Seeing places where kalpas are destroyed, they designate them as having the nature of impermanence; seeing places where kalpas are not destroyed, they designate them as having the nature of ultimate permanence.

These are those who make distinctions by departing from the mind to observe the lands. Third, there are those who observe the subtle and precise movements of the mind, which are capable of giving rise to arising and ceasing. Its...
That which is indestructible is called the nature of permanence. That all birth and death flow forth from the self is called the nature of impermanence;

this is a division into two conceptualizations based upon a single nature. Fourth, because the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) flows on perpetually, it is reckoned as the nature of permanence;

These are those who give rise to partial calculations regarding the four aggregates. They all lose right mindfulness and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi, thereby falling into the ranks of external paths.

The internal faculties and the external vessel-world are all likewise so. To regard arising as finite and cessation as infinite—these are all exhausted paths and lost tracks, resulting from successive false reckonings and the deluded, frantic interpretations of *dhyāna*. Outsiders reckon that the gods are immortal; only by speaking without evasiveness can one be born among these gods. Whenever anyone asks a question, [they respond thus].
He did not dare answer truthfully, fearing that he might fall into evasive confusion. The Buddha said, "This false calculation and empty discourse is indeed evasive confusion.
It has four aspects. The first is evasive confusion resulting from observing transformations while being deluded regarding the principle; this refers to observing the myriad transformations."
Regarding permanence and change, arising and ceasing, increase and decrease, existence and non-existence, they consequently give rise to divergent interpretations.
When questioned, they speak with mutual equivocation, saying that things both arise and cease, and both increase and decrease. Second, observing the locus of cessation, they see mutual non-existence;
yet, while holding in their mouths the answer "non-existent," they engage in equivocation. Third, observing the locus of arising, they see each [thing] individually...

There is. To answer "yes" while holding a contrary position constitutes evasive equivocation (*vāg-vibhramśa*). Fourth, when the mind is inwardly distracted regarding whether an object exists or not, one gives ambiguous and confused responses that can be interpreted either way;
this constitutes evasive equivocation. In all such cases, there is no central principle within, being merely false calculations and empty discourse.
Furthermore, within the continuity of formations, they conceive of future existence, regarding it as the cessation of birth and the arising of death, such that the continuity remains unbroken.
With their minds thus inverted, they conceive: "Form is the self," "The self possesses form," or "Form belongs to the self."
They say, "I am in form," and so on in this cycle. Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness each have sixteen aspects.

They falsely calculate that there is existence after death; furthermore, they may erroneously equate afflictions with awakening, ultimately cycling through these states without ever overcoming or supplanting one another.
All these arise from falsely giving rise to views within the inexhaustible flow.
Furthermore, regarding the cessation of form, feeling, and perception, they give rise to inverted thoughts, reckoning that after death there is nothing.

They say that since form, feeling, and perception have already been extinguished, there is no further continuity; the nature of the aggregates has dissipated—how could there be anything more after death?
There are various characteristics. Because the causes depend on the four aggregates, the present cause perishes and the subsequent fruit is extinguished.

When cause and effect are discussed together, they constitute eight characteristics; after death, both are non-existent. From this, one may deviate into the calculation that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty.

Furthermore, regarding existence and cessation, they calculate eight "neither-nor" [positions] concerning the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): that its existence is a mark of being; that the cessation of form, feeling, perception, and volition is a mark of non-being;

that what exists is ultimately exhausted, and thus though it exists, it is not existent; and that prior to its cessation it previously existed, and thus though it is non-existent, it is not non-existent.
By calculating these four aggregates in pairs, they together constitute eight "neither-nor" positions. Based on this, they further calculate all formations as one.
All [of these] are incorrect. After death, one is in a state of stupor and darkness, such that nothing can be said.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent non-existence, they calculate seven causes for annihilation based on their false conceptualization regarding the locus where the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) perishes moment by moment.

They claim that even if one is born into the seven places of humans and devas, one will subsequently undergo total annihilation. These seven places refer to the two places of humans and devas within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the formless attainments—exhausting the seven limits—all manifest and are extinguished;
once extinguished, they no longer exist.
Furthermore, regarding subsequent states of existence, one calculates five types of nirvāṇa; or, by means of the desire realm, one awakens to the principle of perfect luminosity, and thus...

Taking the desire realm as the locus for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), or alternatively, attaining freedom from sorrow in the first dhyāna, freedom from suffering in the second, supreme bliss in the third, and supreme equanimity in the fourth—this is itself the transformation of the basis into nirvāṇa. [Yet they] do not realize that all these heavens still belong to the outflows (*sāsrava*).

It is not the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), nor is it the ultimate state. These ten kinds of deluded understandings mentioned above are all the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Because the mind and its objects interact, these realizations manifest. This is called the "demon of the mind," which gives rise to deep calamity within oneself. Sentient beings do not recognize this.
Taking delusion for liberation, they claim for themselves that they have attained the state of a sage; having committed a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
(The fifth is the perverse understanding of the meditative absorption [dhyāna] that destroys the consciousness aggregate [vijñānaskandha];

its manifestations are tenfold. "Consciousness" refers to the luminous reflection of a deluded awakening; fundamentally it has no self-substance. It is like a phantom image, empty and non-existent—a perverted and false conceptualization. By means of this...

This serves as its foundation. As for one who cultivates samādhi: when the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted, and one is about to attain great awakening within the heaven of nirvāṇa, the formations cease and consciousness and perception (*vijñāna-darśana*) emerge.
One then profoundly penetrates that the twelve types of dependent and primary retributions throughout the ten directions are all transformations of consciousness;
thus one attains their commonality. By the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, one dissolves the six gates so that the six functions are no longer obstructed, but flow through.
They reflect one another like *vaiḍūrya* crystal, which is transparent and luminous both inside and out; this is the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Such a person then transcends the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). Within this state, there further arise ten kinds of deluded understandings (the *vaiḍūrya* jewel can see objects through mountains).
First, by establishing the cause of true permanence, one becomes a follower of the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) school;
second, by reckoning that the self is born there, one becomes a follower of the "pervasive-perfection" school;
third, by reckoning that it is born from there into the self, one becomes a follower of the "inverted-perfection" school.
1. The fourth consists of calculating that objects each possess a self-nature, which constitutes the seed of perverted cognition.
2. The fifth consists of venerating water and serving fire, which constitutes the seed of deluded transformation. 3.
The sixth consists of calculating eternal extinction based on a substratum—namely, the *nirvāṇa* of non-Buddhists—which constitutes the seed of nihilism.
Seventh, by greedily prolonging the body, one becomes a seed of deluded extension;
eighth, by clinging to desire to solidify life, one becomes a seed of celestial demons;
ninth, by realizing extinction for oneself and resting therein, one becomes a seed of being entangled in emptiness.
Tenth, maintaining awareness to establish the realization of non-transformation and perfecting the seeds:

consciousness flows from formative activity (*saṃskāra*). When activity is empty, consciousness returns to its source. Although birth and death have already been extinguished, one still relies upon the source of consciousness;
therefore, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, it is not yet perfected. One merely refines and dissolves the six gates so that their faculties merge [with their objects].
They are separated from one another; though they employ pure means, they also share a pervasive resonance with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions.
Together they enter the perfect source, nearly returning to the nature of universal penetration. If, regarding this destination, one establishes it as the eternally true, [one remains bound].
If one gives rise to resolute conviction based on causes, that person falls into the attachment to causes and their underlying conditions.
Establishing a mind that seeks attainment and forming a fruit toward which one returns, they oppose perfect penetration and turn their back on Nirvana, giving birth to the seeds of external paths.
Furthermore, by taking that which is grasped as the object of return to be one's own self, one consequently clings to the notion that "I" can produce that [object], yet in reality, one cannot.

Such a person falls into the dualistic clinging of "capacity" and "incapacity. Establishing capacity as the mind, they bring about the fruit of capable activity and generate the seeds of pervasive and perfect [delusion].
Furthermore, because the source of consciousness is what they take as their own refuge, they conversely calculate that it is capable of producing themselves and all dharmas.

Consequently, they identify the place from which things arise and flow forth as the true, eternal, and non-arising essence. While amidst birth and death, they prematurely calculate this to be eternally abiding.
Such a person falls into the attachment of "permanence-in-impermanence," establishing causes based on the mind and thereby forming a falsely conceptualized result.
This is called the "perverted seed of pervasiveness.

Furthermore, they reckon that the substance of cognition is all-pervasive and complete; based on this cognition, they establish their understanding: "The grasses and trees of the ten directions each possess sentience and consciousness, which universally merges with my own cognition.
When wood dies it becomes a human, and when a human dies it becomes wood. Failing to clarify that these are of one substance, they erroneously reckon them to be pervasive and complete.
Such a person falls into the attachment of knowing non-knowing. Calculating the perfectly cognizing mind, they produce the fruit of false delusion and give rise to the seeds of inverted cognition.
Furthermore, within the mutual functioning of the sense organs, they find accord with it and calculate all phenomena—water, fire, wind, and earth—as pure.
The pure radiance circulates and achieves fulfillment, capable of perfect transformation in all things. My own four great elements are entirely subject to it;

yet with a diligent mind, one honors and serves it, hoping to give rise to a superior fruit. Such a person falls into the attachment to birth within non-birth, establishing false causes for their seeking and falsely hoping for fruits.
Thus they produce the seeds of perverted transformation.

Furthermore, within the midst of perfect luminosity, one reckons that the luminosity is empty, thereby destroying the manifold manifestations and returning to a state of eternal stillness as one's refuge.

Not knowing this to be erroneous, such a person falls into the attachment of "returning to the non-returnable. With a perfect emptiness devoid of mind, they produce the fruit of vacuous extinction and give rise to the seed of annihilationism.
Furthermore, within that which is perfect and eternal, one may mistakenly believe that the physical body is identical to that subtle essence and will therefore endure permanently.

Such a person falls into the attachment of craving what is not to be craved; they establish a cause of solid delusion and pursue a fruit of long-term toil (where "toil" refers to the mental suffering of arduous cultivation and unremitting exertion), thereby producing the seeds of delusory prolongation.

Furthermore, they take consciousness as the root of life, which interpenetrates the three periods of time. If the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) were to be exhausted, their transformed life would likewise cease to exist.

Thus, within meditative concentration, they transform various objects of desire while deliberately retaining their defilements so that they do not dissolve; this is done with the intent to realize the true and eternal.

Yet they do not realize it is erroneous; such persons fall into the attachment to the "real" within the unreal. They give rise to the causes of perverse thoughts and establish the effects of blazing afflictions, thus producing the seeds of celestial Māras.

Furthermore, this clarifies the fundamental source from which sentient beings receive their life-destinies: birth and extinction arise from consciousness (*vijñāna*), while refinement and coarseness arise from karma (*karman*).

Therefore, one distinguishes them according to the Four Noble Truths; taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as coarse and false, and cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as refined and true.
To abide in cessation and rest there, no longer advancing further—such a person falls into the category of a śrāvaka of fixed nature. Perfect refinement should be taken as the causal mind.
They achieve the minor fruit of quiescent cessation; taking little as sufficient, they realize partial truth and give rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
Furthermore, regarding the perfectly interfused, pure, and luminous awakening, they investigate it as profound and subtle, establishing it as a realized fruit, yet they do not advance further.
Such a person falls into the fixed-nature pratyekabuddha; they take the perfect awakening as their causal mind and achieve a state of tranquil clarity.

Stagnant fruits arise as the awakening becomes perfectly luminous, yet they do not transform into perfect seeds. Thus, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* may lead to madness midway through the practice due to reliance on delusion;

within what is not yet sufficient, one gives rise to the realization of sufficiency. All of these belong to the *vijñāna-skandha*. Because the mind is applied in a state of mutual conflict, this stage arises.
For those who cultivate *samādhi*, once the consciousness-mind is exhausted, the various faculties function interchangeably. At this point—

Within the mutual application [of these practices], one is able to enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine *śuṣka-vipaśyanā* (dry wisdom). With a perfectly luminous and refined mind, transformation is manifested therein, like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.
In this way, one transcends the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the four minds of preparatory application.
One then enters the Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten adamantine grounds (*bhūmi*), attaining the perfect luminosity of Equal Enlightenment. Thus, one enters...
The Tathāgata’s Ocean of Sublime Adornments is perfected in Bodhi and returns to non-attainment.
Chapter Thirty: The Final Inquiry.
Ānanda asked: "Regarding the five kinds of delusion within the characteristics of the five aggregates, are they to be eliminated simultaneously, or in succession?"
[The interlocutor asks: "Exhausted thus in five layers, what constitutes their boundary? The Buddha replied: "The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have delusion as their root.
As for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), its root is solidified deluded thought (*abhiniveśa-vikalpa*). Your physical body, O disciple, was first caused by the deluded thoughts of your parents.

If your mind were not characterized by thought, it would be unable to transmit life within the realm of thought—just as saliva flows at the mere thought of vinegar, or as the feet ache from the mere thought of climbing a height."

It is precisely because the substance [of the body] is bound by delusion that it can participate in the same category as delusion; life is transmitted through perception—this is exactly what is meant.

As for the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), as previously described regarding the delusory thoughts when facing heights, it can cause your physical substance to actually experience bitterness and astringency.
Thus, the two types of objects before you—those favorable and those adverse—are fundamentally all illusory, and they can likewise cause your material body [to experience such sensations].
In reality, there is neither loss nor gain; therefore, it is said that empty clarity and false conceptualization constitute its root.

It is due to your thoughts and deliberations that your physical body appears inconsistent in its substantiality and insubstantiality, yet these can mutually influence one another so that thought and form merge. Thus, the mind gives rise to empty images.
Form is capable of producing completion. Although the mind and form have different functions, they are able to correspond; it is *saṃjñā* (perception/conceptualization) that connects them.
As for waking and sleeping, or movement and change, the ability to cause the mind to follow objects in arising and objects to follow the mind in changing is due to *saṃjñā*.
Therefore, *saṃjñā* is the fundamental basis of pervasive delusive conceptualization. Its transformative principle shifts subtly, with day and night succeeding one another.
"You do not realize this yourself. If this were not you, how could its essence undergo change? This must be your true self; why then are you unaware of it?
Therefore, practitioners take these obscure and hidden delusions as their foundation.

Furthermore, because you identify that which is refined, true, and profoundly still—as unchanging, if it were truly refined and true, it would not admit of delusive habituation. Yet now, you are able to conceal your former [nature]."
"Recorded": that which one sees once and never forgets is precisely the habit-energy of delusion (*vāsanā*).

Thus, within this state of exquisite stillness and immovability, every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) undergoes perfuming (*vāsana*), and seeds are deposited within consciousness (*vijñāna*); there is ample room for delusion. One should know that this clarity is not true clarity;
it is merely a state of profound concealment and latency, remaining unnoticed. It is like a torrential stream that appears tranquil at first glance, yet is [in fact] rushing.
It is not that there is no outflow; rather, it is that one does not perceive the outflow. This is the source of true recollection and the substance of the containment of delusion.

Therefore it is said: "Consciousness (vijñāna) takes the formless and the void as its basis. One must simply exhaust the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) and dissolve the six sense-gates, so that deluded habits have nowhere to lodge;
only then can the nature of habituation be extinguished. These five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandhāḥ) are the five delusions.
The perception is established. Originally there is no realm; it arises due to the cause of delusive appearances. Form is not form by itself; it exists because of emptiness.
Only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form. Separation is not separation by itself; it exists because of contact. Only contact and separation [constitute the limit of separation].

This is the limit of sensation (*vedanā*): it is forgotten yet not forgotten of its own accord; because of memory there is forgetting. Only memory and forgetting—this is the limit of perception (*saṃjñā*):

it ceases yet does not cease of its own accord; because of arising there is cessation. Only cessation and arising—this constitutes the limit of mental formations (*saṃskāra*): it is tranquil yet does not become tranquil of its own accord;
because mental activity does not flow away, the nature enters primordial clarity and accords with profound lucidity. This constitutes the limit of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
These five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) fundamentally arise in layers. Their arising is caused by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and their cessation begins with the removal of form (*rūpa*).

In principle, they are realized all at once through sudden enlightenment; yet, as one rides upon this realization, they are simultaneously dissolved. In practice, however, they are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through a gradual process. Guishan said:

"Arising proceeds from the internal to the external, from the subtle to the coarse, like putting on clothes. Thus, when deluded regarding the principle, there is consciousness, and so on, up to [form]."

Regarding form (*rūpa*): its cessation proceeds from the external to the internal, and from the coarse to the subtle, like the shedding of garments. Thus, one realizes that as the principle is understood, form is exhausted, continuing until consciousness (*vijñāna*) is exhausted.
The Exegesis of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra (Concluded)
